extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, elementary classroom teachers, and assessment specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric and measurement criteria for assessing third- and fourth-grade students' mathematical and procedural writing (and comparing written to oral mathematical explanations). Focuses on quantitative and qualitative indicators used in a classroom research study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of words written
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses the number of words a child writes in response to a prompt as a basis for comparison and evaluation; prior work found number of words (and clauses) correlated significantly with mean ratings of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors grouped samples into three bands (low 0–50, medium 51–100, high 101–175 words). Because of small n in the high group, medium and high were combined for analysis. Correlation reported between number of words and rubric quality score (r = .5313, p = .0192). Cited support: Berninger et al. (1992) and Bereiter & Scardamalia (1978,1979).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric quality score (10-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric was used to analyze writing prompts with regard to the quality of the writing; the rubric produces a numeric score (10-point scale was used in reported comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same rubric was applied to written samples and to transcripts of oral responses. Differences of 1–5 points on the 10-point scale were observed between oral and written scores in favor of oral. Rubric details (rubric items) are not fully reproduced in the report but the rubric was treated as a holistic/analytic quality measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: General writing ability (domain-free procedural writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' performance on domain-free (procedural) writing prompts reflects their general writing ability and is predictive of mathematical writing performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A significant main effect of general writing ability on mathematical writing (based on number of words) was recorded (p = 0.0011), supporting caution when inferring mathematical understanding solely from mathematical writing products because general writing skill influences written articulation of mathematical processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt cognitive level (procedural sequence, idea generation/explanation, application/problem generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical prompts were designed to elicit different levels of thinking: (1) procedural sequences for solving problem-types, (2) generation and explanation of important ideas relevant to the concept, and (3) creation of problems using the concept in application contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers used three mathematical prompts representing these levels but analyzed only two (procedural sequence and idea-generation/explanation) because of inconsistent prompt execution. Choice of prompt type is a deliberate evaluative dimension to elicit procedural vs conceptual responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality comparison: oral vs written expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison between oral explanations (transcripts) and written responses as alternate modalities for expressing mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In every instance the rubric score for oral expression surpassed written expression (by 1–5 points), despite spoken responses having fewer words on average. Suggests oral modality may reveal understanding that written products underrepresent due to mechanical/transcription constraints; therefore modality should be considered in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/transcription constraints on written responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that mechanical aspects of writing (handwriting, transcription, difficulty putting concepts into words) can limit the adequacy of written products to reflect conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note mechanical constraints may explain lower written rubric scores and recommend caution in using written products as the primary basis for assessing mathematical understanding; this factor should be considered when interpreting writing-based assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and syntactical/linguistic expression of mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Completeness of concept expression and syntactical/linguistic usage are important dimensions of quality for mathematical writing (though not fully analyzed in this study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The present analysis did not include measures such as syntactical usage or completeness of expression; authors indicate these will be studied in future examinations and imply they are substantive rubric dimensions to evaluate mathematical writing quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain knowledge / topic familiarity as a driver of writing fluency
rubrics_metrics.description: Students write more fluently and produce stronger written output when writing about topics they know well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on McCutchen (1986), two baseline 'domain-free' procedural prompts were included (write about something you do well; how to play a favorite game) to measure general writing fluency versus mathematical-topic-specific writing. Implication: assessors should account for topic familiarity when interpreting writing performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental stage of writing (writing developmental stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's stage of writing development (e.g., undifferentiated, differentiated, ideographic, etc.) influences their written products and must be taken into account when evaluating writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors reference Klein (1985) and Vygotskian/Piagetian frameworks describing overlapping stages of writing development; evaluators should consider developmental writing stage (not only chronological age) as it affects the nature and adequacy of written mathematical explanations.
